newsitem.title: FRANCE: Stunned survivors tell of Algeria's night bloodbath.
newsitem.headline: Stunned survivors tell of Algeria's night bloodbath.

text.p: Stunned survivors of Algeria's worst massacre in five years of slaughter told in tearful testimony published on Wednesday how Moslem rebels mercilessly hacked and shot 93 people to death in a night-long bloodbath.
Nearly half of the dead were women and young girls.
Their throats were cut, heads hacked off and others shot in an orgy of savagery 25 km (15 miles) from the capital Algiers that ended only as dawn approached on Tuesday.

"When they left, I got up. And there in the yard was only blood, bloodied bodies and heads everywhere. I fainted," said 14-year-old Radia, who had pretended to be dead as her whole family was slaughtered.
Witnesses quoted by Algerian newspapers said between 40 and 50 men took part in the raid on an isolated farming community, Haouch Boughlef-Khemisti, in Bougara district.
"A bomb explosion woke us...Some minutes later they started dragging us to the centre of the village where they began cutting people's throats," said 33-year-old Houria.

"One held my head and another my clothes and they sliced my throat quickly. I fainted...one of them came and kicked me to see if I was really dead," she said in her account in the newspaper Al-Khabar. "My husband was killed, his throat cut."

The government termed the massacre one of unprecedented savagery and said the killers, some of whom had been shot by intervening security forces, were being hunted down. Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia vowed "terrorism" would be eliminated.
"This is a savage act such as mankind has never before witnessed," he said on television.

Opposition Socialist Forces Front spokesman Ali Rachedi, on state radio on Wednesday, called on Ouyahia to quit. "Ouyahia repeatedly said the security situation improved and the government had won over terrorism. The massacre showed that this was not true."

Ahmed Dane, spokesman for Hamas, the main legal Islamist party, said: "Instead of appearing on television to deplore the massacre, it would be more decent of government head Ouyahia to step down after his failure to guarantee security."
The latest massacre, in which three children aged nine months to four years were killed, brought to nearly 300 the number killed in recent weeks in similar raids.

It coincided with the deadline for candidates to register for the first parliamentary elections since authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which Moslem fundamentalists had taken a commanding lead. The country plunged into violence in which about 60,000 people have since died.
Officials expect 4,000 to have registered for the poll.
One diplomatic source in the Algerian capital Algiers said the violence seemed to have increased since the June 5 election date was set, but there was no hard evidence to link them.
Another added: "It's possible it's linked to the elections but it could just be a continuation of efforts to destabilise the country, or even to vendettas (between rival groups)."
Another commentator in Algiers said: "It appears the killing was perpetrated because the village had refused to provide food for the terrorists."
Former colonial power France said on Wednesday it was "worried and shocked by the blind and savage nature of the violence hitting Algeria."
On Tuesday the bodies were taken to the canteen of the local school, as earthmovers dug graves in the cemetery. Hundreds of people from the area attended the funerals.
On Wednesday, 25 wounded who had survived lay in hospital, 18 in a serious condition. One survivor, Mohamed, who saw the attackers cut off his brother's head, asked: "My God, why us?"
